Fly me to the Moon

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
.....a new race to the Moon is underway

Unique Selling Point:
This is a new development in space exploration -- humans are going backs to the Moon and this time it is not just Nasa but several nations and private companies.

Summary:
On 4 June, SpaceX's Crew Dragon Capsule was blasted into space and docked with the international space station. All amazing and spectacular stuff.

However, few people realise that developing rockets and spacecraft by private individuals and not only governments, are part of a new race to the Moon.

Further information:
On 4 June, SpaceX's Crew Dragon Capsule was blasted into space and docked with the international space station. All amazing and spectacular stuff.

However, few people realise that developing rockets and spacecraft by private individuals and not only governments, are part of a new race to the Moon.

One tends to think that the Moon has been explored by the US only, but that is not true. So far, the US, The Russians, China, India, Japan and Israel have all landed on the moon and explored it so some extent. (OK the both the Isreali and Indian crafts crash landed on the Moon and were destroyed, but they are going back).

And private companies like SpaceX (Musk) and Blue Origin (Bezos) also have the moon firmly in their sights.

Donald Trump has announced that the US will land astronauts on the Moon in 2023.

But why this renewed interest in the Moon? There are a number of reasons, and all very interesting. Scientists and Governments are looking towards the Moon for things like:

* New technologies (materials, AI, computers, 3D printing, etc.) makes it much easier to achieve, and even private companies are now looking at landing on the Moon.

* Ice/Water. Found in great quantities at the moon’s poles, water could be converted into fuel for spacecraft. It could also be a source of oxygen and liquid water, making it vastly easier to build and sustain human habitation on the moon.

* Helium-3. It’s a nonradioactive isotope, or variant, of helium and is believed to be a clean source of nuclear energy. Solar winds deposit it on the moon. Twenty-five tons of helium-3 would provide enough energy to power the U.S. for a year, some scientists say.

* Mining the Moon. Driving the new space race is a potent mix of economic, technological and geopolitical imperatives. There are possible fortunes to be made from lunar ventures. Space-based businesses currently contribute $350 billion to the global gross domestic product, a figure projected to jump to $1.4 trillion by 2040, according to Morgan Stanley.

* A new Space station in lunar orbit. NASA plans to put a small space station, called Gateway, in lunar orbit.

* Homesteading -- a permanent base on the moon. This will serve to mine the moon and also as a way station for future travel to Mars. Any road to Mars likely runs straight through the moon. Homesteading a world that is only three days from Earth is the best way to test the life-support infrastructure that would be needed on a far more distant—and a good deal less barren planet.

Interviewees: Variety of international space experts and people from South Africa's Space Agency

* Rick Tumlinson, space pioneer. Called one of the top space “Visionaries” on the planet, Rick is also considered to be a “Godfather” of the space revolution of Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and a new generation of space pioneers. His ideas and projects helped create the framework for the current move to open the High Frontier. From leading a team that took over the Mir Space station for a year to selling the first ticket to the ISS and helping start the search for water ice on the Moon, Rick has set the course for our breakout into space.

* Dr Valanathan Munsami, Head of the South African National Space Agency

* Dr Eugene Avenant, Chief Engineer at SANSA, running the Hartebeeshoek facility.

* Dr Jill Stuart is an academic based at the London School of Economics and Political Science. She is an expert in the politics, ethics and law of outer space exploration and exploitation. She is a frequent presence in the global media (print, radio, television, documentary) and regularly gives lectures around the world.

There is a lot of visual material available from all of the agencies, all Nasa footage and images and animations are in the public domain, China has a lot in the public domain as well.

The technologies being developed is fantastic but the social implication and the geopolitical ramifications are as interesting and relevant in the world that is moving into a new world order.

Another layer is that of nations or individuals laying claim to the mineral resources in the solar system. The current Outer Space Treaty only prohibits ownership of celestial bodies and say nothing about the exploitation of natural resources.

Dr. Valanathan Munsami
Mr. Rick Tumlinson
Dr. Jill Stuart

Press Release:


The New Race to the Moon
SpaceX's Crew Dragon Capsule has docked with the International Space Station and this week started a series of spacewalks to swap out ageing nickel-hydrogen batteries for smaller, efficient lithium-ion batteries. As Earth’s resources take strain, Carte Blanche examines what lies behind the efforts of private corporations to develop rockets to get to the moon. With rich deposits of water ice that can be turned into fuel for space missions – is the moon now fit for human settlement and as a waystation for space-travel?


Script:


TEXT on screen
Fifty one years ago in the far away Milky Way Galaxy people from Planet Earth sent 12 men to the planet’s Moon. Decades have passed and now they are planning to go back.
V/O:
On the 30th of May, a worldwide audience watched spellbound as a SpaceX rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral with two astronauts on board. It was the first manned launch from American soil in 9 years, and it received massive media coverage.
LINK:
What makes this launch so significant is that it was done by a private company and not a Government agency. And what is more – it is just a precursor of things to come.
V/O:
The things to come include not only landing humans briefly on the Moon again, but also to establish a permanent base on the lunar surface.

Rick Tumlinson is a space entrepreneur and space activist; he has co-founded several space companies and supports the new drive to get to the Moon and to Mars.
Mac:
And the possibilities of having permanent habitat on the Moon. Is that something that is in the foreseeable far future?
Rick:
I would say that it is in the foreseeable near future. We will have human communities on the Moon, probably starting in the next ten years or so.
V/O:
The first step to achieve this is to land humans on the Moon again, and this could happen very soon, says Dr Val Munsami, CEO of the South African National Space Agency.
Munsami:
The US through Nasa made this a mission of getting back to the Moon. So, it is the first woman who will land on the moon and the next man and that will be in 2024.
V/O:
Nasa calls this the Artemis project.

However, Nasa astronauts might not be the first humans to return to the Moon. That is because a new race to the Moon is underway, and many countries and private companies have also set their sights on landing humans on the lunar surface.

In fact, apart from the United States, Russia, Japan, Israel, China, and India have all sent unmanned landers to the Moon in recent years.

And the South African National Space Agency has also been involved in the new race to the moon. They provided assistance to the Indian mission by tracking the rocket after launch and received and recorded data during the mission.
Munsami:
That mission was actually supported from here, from this site, form SANSA. We supported it from the launch right up till getting on the Moon.
V/O:
In the 1970’s the South African National Space Agency also supported the some of the Apollo missions to the Moon. The facility at Hartebeeshoek tracks satellites and rockets as they come over South Africa and record the data on behalf of agencies and private clients.

They also have a space weather station in Hermanus where they track activity on the Sun. They are also in the process of designing and building satellites.

China has become the first nation that managed to land a rover on the far side of the Moon. This is what it looks like on the part of the Moon that we never see.

Many believe having a permanent human presence on the Moon will provide humanity with all kinds of interesting possibilities.
Rick:
If you are going to establish a monastery – it is a pretty quiet place, you know. The idea that you could go and stay in a hotel built into the cliff-side from of the crater, with the earth sitting in front of you, that could be quite interesting.
V/O
But far more than the possibility of space tourism, the Moon is also seen as the gateway to explore Mars and rest of the solar system. And it is because of one simple reason: there is ice in the craters at the lunar poles.
Rick:
Ice, Hydrogen and Oxygen, and its various combinations, is in a sense the gold of the inner solar system. If you have ice, you have water, you can freeze the ice and use it to shield you from radiation, you can break it up and have Oxygen to breathe, and you can create other compounds such as methanol and plastics and things like that. And if you light Oxygen and Hydrogen you have rocket propellant.
V/O:
What gave the race to the Moon further impetus is that private companies are able to reduce the cost of getting cargo and humans into space dramatically.

For example, SpaceX’s reusable rockets have dropped the cost of sending a kilogram of cargo into space from fifty-four thousand dollars to about three thousand dollars.

In addition, over the last 10 years or so launching satellites has become a massive commercial enterprise. This has lured many private companies to become interested in space, the Moon and Mars. These include Elon Musk’s SpaceX, Jeff Bizos’ Blue Origin and Moon Express.

There are enormous commercial benefits in mining on the Moon for minerals and metals that are scarce on Earth, or of which there are dwindling resources on the planet.

And, there is Helium-3 on the Moon. It is a rare Helium isotope and it is believed it could be the answer to all the energy needs of Planet Earth. A nuclear fusion reaction of Helium-3 atoms releases enormous amounts of clean energy.

Rick:
One large spacecraft-load of Helium-3 brought back to the earth will probably satisfy all of our needs for a long time.
V/O:
And just few kilograms of Helium-3 could be worth trillions of dollars.

In addition to mining the Moon, the idea is that the Moon also becomes a fuel depot for missions further into space, including going to Mars. The red planet has long been on the agenda of many space programmes.
LINK:
This year, in August Nasa will send a new rover to Mars. It will arrive in February 2021 and will drill into the planet.
V/O:
It will be the 15th probe on the Martian surface and will explore for minerals. Humans could follow within 10 years.

A moon base will also facilitate the mining of asteroids for all kinds of resources such as precious metals.

The big question of course is – will mining the Moon and asteroids be legal?

At the London School of Economics, Dr Jill Stuart specializes in the politics, ethics and law of outer space exploration and exploitation.
Jill:
Who owns the resources in space? This is a very hot topic. The Outer Space treaty of 1967 is sometimes referred to as the Outer Space Constitution, and what is says is that Outer Space basically belong s to no one and to everyone at the same time. So, no individual country can pay claim to any celestial territory and also Outer Space is the common heritage of mankind.
V/O:
But when the treaty was created, mining resources on the moon or asteroids was not on the table. But now it is a distinct possibility. So much so that numerous countries are scurrying to legislate ownership of extra-terrestrial resources.
LINK:
Many people believe that establishing a permanent on celestial bodies could be a repeat of the devastation that humans have caused on earth.
V/O:
However, some believe it could be a new beginning
Rick:
We have devastated this planet. The expansion of human civilization has been an ongoing and perpetual attack against the rest of the ecosphere on this planet. However, as we move into the deadness of space it is a complete reversal of the paradigm, because for the first time in human history, we are going to be expanding the domain of life and hopefully taking the pressure off of the earth.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: This is a new development in space exploration -- humans are going backs to the Moon and this time it is not just Nasa but several nations and private companies.
metadata.Summary: On 4 June, SpaceX's Crew Dragon Capsule was blasted into space and docked with the international space station. All amazing and spectacular stuff. However, few people realise that developing rockets and spacecraft by private individuals and not only governments, are part of a new race to the Moon.
metadata.Further information: On 4 June, SpaceX's Crew Dragon Capsule was blasted into space and docked with the international space station. All amazing and spectacular stuff. However, few people realise that developing rockets and spacecraft by private individuals and not only governments, are part of a new race to the Moon. One tends to think that the Moon has been explored by the US only, but that is not true. So far, the US, The Russians, China, India, Japan and Israel have all landed on the moon and explored it so some extent. (OK the both the Isreali and Indian crafts crash landed on the Moon and were destroyed, but they are going back). And private companies like SpaceX (Musk) and Blue Origin (Bezos) also have the moon firmly in their sights. Donald Trump has announced that the US will land astronauts on the Moon in 2023. But why this renewed interest in the Moon? There are a number of reasons, and all very interesting. Scientists and Governments are looking towards the Moon for things like: * New technologies (materials, AI, computers, 3D printing, etc.) makes it much easier to achieve, and even private companies are now looking at landing on the Moon. * Ice/Water. Found in great quantities at the moon’s poles, water could be converted into fuel for spacecraft. It could also be a source of oxygen and liquid water, making it vastly easier to build and sustain human habitation on the moon. * Helium-3. It’s a nonradioactive isotope, or variant, of helium and is believed to be a clean source of nuclear energy. Solar winds deposit it on the moon. Twenty-five tons of helium-3 would provide enough energy to power the U.S. for a year, some scientists say. * Mining the Moon. Driving the new space race is a potent mix of economic, technological and geopolitical imperatives. There are possible fortunes to be made from lunar ventures. Space-based businesses currently contribute $350 billion to the global gross domestic product, a figure projected to jump to $1.4 trillion by 2040, according to Morgan Stanley. * A new Space station in lunar orbit. NASA plans to put a small space station, called Gateway, in lunar orbit. * Homesteading -- a permanent base on the moon. This will serve to mine the moon and also as a way station for future travel to Mars. Any road to Mars likely runs straight through the moon. Homesteading a world that is only three days from Earth is the best way to test the life-support infrastructure that would be needed on a far more distant—and a good deal less barren planet. Interviewees: Variety of international space experts and people from South Africa's Space Agency * Rick Tumlinson, space pioneer. Called one of the top space “Visionaries” on the planet, Rick is also considered to be a “Godfather” of the space revolution of Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and a new generation of space pioneers. His ideas and projects helped create the framework for the current move to open the High Frontier. From leading a team that took over the Mir Space station for a year to selling the first ticket to the ISS and helping start the search for water ice on the Moon, Rick has set the course for our breakout into space. * Dr Valanathan Munsami, Head of the South African National Space Agency * Dr Eugene Avenant, Chief Engineer at SANSA, running the Hartebeeshoek facility. * Dr Jill Stuart is an academic based at the London School of Economics and Political Science. She is an expert in the politics, ethics and law of outer space exploration and exploitation. She is a frequent presence in the global media (print, radio, television, documentary) and regularly gives lectures around the world. There is a lot of visual material available from all of the agencies, all Nasa footage and images and animations are in the public domain, China has a lot in the public domain as well. The technologies being developed is fantastic but the social implication and the geopolitical ramifications are as interesting and relevant in the world that is moving into a new world order. Another layer is that of nations or individuals laying claim to the mineral resources in the solar system. The current Outer Space Treaty only prohibits ownership of celestial bodies and say nothing about the exploitation of natural resources.
